analysis.one_liner: Adds eyeglasses, hearing aids, and dental care to Medicare coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill won 132 sponsors but never got a committee vote or floor action in the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare today does not cover eyeglasses, hearing aids, or most dental care, and the law specifically lists them as excluded. This bill would delete those exclusions, so seniors' Medicare would pay for glasses, hearing aids, and dental services. It was referred to two House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors on Medicare, who currently pay out of pocket for glasses, hearing aids (often several thousand dollars a pair), and dental work. Roughly 60 million people are on Medicare [widely known]; the bill would shift those costs to the Medicare program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors needing vision, hearing, or dental care

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the statutory exclusion of eyeglasses and hearing aids from Medicare coverage, so the program would pay for them [S3].
Deletes the statutory exclusion of dental services from Medicare coverage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare program and its taxpayers and beneficiaries, through higher federal health spending; no offsetting funding source is specified in the bill.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no funding mechanism or offset; expanding coverage to glasses, hearing aids, and dental care would add significant federal spending with no stated way to pay for it [S3].

Opponents of expanding Medicare benefits generally argue that mandatory benefit additions raise premiums and program costs for everyone, including seniors who don't need these services; this objection was not formally recorded because the bill never got a hearing or vote [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial and concrete: hearing aids and dental work are among the largest out-of-pocket costs seniors face, and Medicare excludes all of them by statute. The cost is also real — this would be one of the largest expansions of Medicare benefits in decades with no financing mechanism in the bill — but the bill never advanced far enough for the cost debate to happen on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees — with a subcommittee referral — and died there when the 115th Congress ended; neither committee ever voted on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced January 12, 2017 and referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
On January 31, 2017 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S5].
It accumulated 131 cosponsors, 130 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seniors keep paying out of pocket for glasses, hearing aids, and dental care; no interest group lost anything because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Seniors' out-of-pocket costs stayed the same

for.name: Lucille Roybal-Allard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand Medicare to cover eyeglasses, hearing aids, and dental care [S1][S3].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or vote on it appears in the record [S5].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral (jurisdiction over Medicare)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or vote on it appears in the record [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was almost entirely Democratic — 130 Democrats and 1 Republican among 132 total supporters [S4].

industries.industry: Medicare beneficiaries' out-of-pocket providers (hearing aid makers, optical retailers, dental practices)
industries.note: A Medicare benefit for glasses, hearing aids, and dental care would create a large new paying customer base for these providers — with the cost borne by Medicare rather than seniors directly [S3].

Many Advantage plans already offer limited vision and dental extras as marketing perks; a universal Medicare benefit would reduce that differentiation even as overall program spending grew. This effect is inferred from how the market works, not from the bill text [S3].
